title: Al Jackson Jr. - Wikipedia
notes: Albert J. Jackson Jr., born 27 November 1935, Memphis; died 1 October 1975, Memphis, shot at home by an intruder, never identified. His father Al Jackson Sr. led a jazz and swing dance band; on stage with it from 1940, aged five. Willie Mitchell's band while also in the Ben Branch band (Mitchell: 'Al Junior was about 14 years old then'; 'swinging that damn band like a pro'). Cropper and Dunn heard him with Mitchell at the Flamingo Room; Booker T. Jones: 'You guys need to know about Al.' Stax's first salaried session musician; kept playing Hi sessions for Mitchell. 'The Human Timekeeper'; 'an instantly recognizable backbeat'. Co-wrote and played on Al Green hits (Let's Stay Together, I'm Still in Love with You). Sessions: Elvis Presley, Bill Withers, Wilson Pickett, Eric Clapton (461 Ocean Boulevard), Aretha Franklin (Young, Gifted and Black), Rod Stewart (Atlantic Crossing), Ann Peebles, Donny Hathaway and others. Gear: 'combinations of Ludwig and Rogers drums and Zildjian cymbals'; a Ludwig kit with a Rogers Powertone snare from Stax at the Musicians Hall of Fame; a Rogers kit with a Ludwig Acrolite snare from Hi at the Stax Museum; Cropper (in Jim Payne's Give the Drummer Some!) on a grey pearl Rogers floor tom in the mix-and-match Stax kit. Memphis Music Hall of Fame 2015; Rock and Roll Hall of Fame 1992 with the M.G.'s.

title: Booker T. & the M.G.'s - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 110,492. Formed summer 1962 at Stax: Jones, Cropper, Lewie Steinberg, Jackson, jamming during a Billy Lee Riley session; Green Onions No. 1 R&B, No. 3 pop. Dunn replaced Steinberg in 1965. Stax/Volt Revue tour of Europe, spring 1967; Monterey Pop, June 1967, their own set and then backing Otis Redding. Soul Limbo, Hang 'Em High, Time Is Tight (No. 6); McLemore Avenue (1970); Melting Pot (1971). Cropper: Jackson was 'the greatest drummer to ever walk the earth.' Rock and Roll Hall of Fame 1992; Grammy Lifetime Achievement 2007.

title: Memphis Music Hall of Fame: Al Jackson Jr.
notes: Inducted 2015. Quotes gathered there: Booker T. Jones, 'He would hit you over the head with the drumstick if one eighth note or a sixteenth note was off'; Willie Mitchell (to Drum! Magazine), 'He could play Gene Krupa and all that stuff. And he was reading charts when he was 12 years old'; Duck Dunn, 'With Al you just had to kind of wait on him and wait till he'd come down on the beat to catch him ... He'd just keep it right where he thought it should be and he'd make you look like a fool. But he was right ninety per cent of the time'; Al Green (Rolling Stone, 1973), 'He'll stay back there for hours, just beating the drums with his eyes closed', and that he would go to Jamaica or the Bahamas for days 'to pick up on some kind of rhythm'; Cropper, 'He defined the groove, the beat, the mood, everything. You listen to Al Jackson and you played accordingly'.

title: Drummer Cafe: Al Jackson Jr.
notes: No byline. 'The Human Timekeeper'; Green Onions 'should be in every drummer's arsenal'. 'To dampen his snare drum, Jackson always used his wallet'; 'He never changed the drumheads unless one broke'; the Stax kit 'always remained set up and mic'd'; two mics, one an RCA 44 on the bass drum with the front head on, the front head sometimes removed in later years; a 5x14 Ludwig Acrolite live in the 1960s. Kit list: Rogers, all black: 14x20 bass drum, 8x12 tom, 16x16 floor tom, 5x14 Rogers Powertone 8-lug wood snare; Zildjian 14-inch hi-hats, 16-inch crash, 18-inch ride. Unsourced; read as a summary of the usual accounts.

title: Modern Drummer, 'Al Jackson', 29 March 2010
notes: No byline; read through a summary, so not quoted. Stax house band; with his father's big band at five; several years in Willie Mitchell's band before the M.G.'s (1962); often the last word on feel, tempo and groove at the day's sessions; 'deceptively simple'; few fills and no unneeded crashes, so the arrangement was not washed out; beats tailored to each tune; a spacious, clean, strong sound; Al Green at Hi as drummer and co-writer; non-Stax records for Aretha Franklin, Bill Withers, Leon Russell, Rod Stewart.

title: Vinnie Sperrazza, 'On Backbeats', Chronicles (Substack), 8 August 2024
notes: Quotes Ethan Iverson's 'In Search of the Backbeat' (The Nation, August 2024), where Steve Jordan names the backbeat's greatest proponents, among them 'Al Jackson Jr. of the Stax Records house band and Al Green's band at Hi Records'. Sperrazza, a drummer: of Jackson and Benny Benjamin, 'we can hear their deep jazz background plain as day'. Green Onions: 'Jackson's elemental beat is slick, clean, and perfectly in time. No fills, no variations, just subtle dynamics and intense focus.' Let's Stay Together: 'On the verses, Jackson's left hand plays the backbeat on the snare as usual' while the right hand moves 'from the hi-hat to a muffled floor tom to play the backbeat in unison with the snare', 'softening the backbeat'.

title: Robert Doerschuk, 'Sam Moore Remembers Al Jackson Jr.', Traps, Spring 2007 (reposted on Substack, 27 August 2024)
notes: Sam Moore: 'This man was like a human metronome. He had tempo'; 'Al could lay down a pattern, and he would follow you wherever you wanted to go'; 'He was the best setup man you could ever find'; 'You don't count! Al is doing that for you!'; 'He's got his foot on the sock, holding it down, and he's playing the snare with one hand'; 'Buddy Rich played double bass. Al played single'; 'Al is playing subtle'; 'Al and Isaac, that was the sound of Sam & Dave and Otis Redding'; When Something Is Wrong with My Baby took sixty-five takes. Doerschuk: 'when you play less, you can lock in more effectively'; 'his knowledge of where to drop that rare fill'.

title: Todd Bishop, 'Groove o' the day: Al Jackson, Jr. - Crosscut Saw', Cruise Ship Drummer!, 30 December 2014
notes: Albert King, Born Under a Bad Sign. 'A sort of a blues rhumba groove'; no hi-hat on the record; 'Play the housetop accents as rim shots'; the bass drum slightly accented on 2 and 4, and on 2 and 4 only in the last chorus; the bass drum often accents 1 at new sections. The notation itself is an image and was not read.

title: Todd Bishop, 'Transcription: Al Jackson - Over Easy', Cruise Ship Drummer!, 16 August 2013
notes: Booker T. & the M.G.'s, the build-up from 2:38, busier than his custom: the hat played with the left hand while the ride continues; the snare at three levels (accent, normal, ghost); sixteenth-note triplets and sextuplets 'probably RRL'; a fill ended 'strongly with the bass drum only', then back in on beat 2 at a softer level. The notation is an image and was not read.

title: Andy McDonough, 'Gearing Up: Inside The Stax Sound', American Songwriter, 15 July 2016
notes: 'The biggest part of the drum sound at Stax would have to be attributed to drummer, Al Jackson, Jr.'; 'a Rogers kit mostly, and a chrome-plated Ludwig Supraphonic 400 snare'; the Memphis trick of 'taping a wallet to the top head'; 'a very small booth for drums', so little room sound; often only a Neumann KM-84 on the snare at up to eight inches, one U-87 overhead, perhaps an RE-20 on the bass drum, the hi-hat almost never miked; bass, bass drum and snare often shared track one. The studio practice is the room's, not said to be his alone.

title: Alan Richard, 'End of the Groove', Salvation South, 4 March 2022
notes: Howard Grimes's obituary. Jackson was 'the other regular drummer in the Hi Rhythm Section'; he drums on Ann Peebles' I Can't Stand the Rain; on Let's Stay Together 'Al Jackson handled the drums, but Howard played the little gallop that helped make it a classic.'

title: Allison Rapp, Howard Grimes obituary, Ultimate Classic Rock, 14 February 2022
notes: Says Grimes was 'tutored by Al Jackson Jr.' at Stax and took over as Hi's main drummer when Jackson died in 1975. Grimes himself disputed being tutored ('I was before Al Jackson', reported in search summaries of his memoir Timekeeper, not read), so no teacher edge is drawn.

title: In the Midnight Hour - Wikipedia
notes: Wilson Pickett, recorded 12 May 1965 at Stax, Memphis; Al Jackson Jr. on drums. Cropper credits Jerry Wexler with the 'delayed backbeat': Wexler demonstrated the Jerk; 'they were putting the accent on two'; 'Basically, we'd been one-beat-accenters with an afterbeat.'

title: Green Onions - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded June 1962, Memphis; Jones (Hammond M3), Cropper, Lewie Steinberg, Al Jackson Jr. on drums; a twelve-bar blues; No. 3 Hot 100, No. 1 R&B.

title: Green Onions (album) - Wikipedia
notes: October 1962, Stax's first album, produced by Jim Stewart, recorded June to August 1962 at Stax; Jones, Cropper, Steinberg, Jackson.

title: Otis Blue/Otis Redding Sings Soul - Wikipedia
notes: Volt, 15 September 1965; recorded 9-10 July 1965 at Stax; produced by Jim Stewart and Steve Cropper; Al Jackson Jr. the only drummer credited; Respect, I've Been Loving You Too Long, Shake, Satisfaction.

title: Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary of Soul - Wikipedia
notes: Volt, October 1966; produced by Jim Stewart; Al Jackson Jr. on drums; includes Try a Little Tenderness, whose cymbal break near the peak was arranged by Isaac Hayes.

title: Born Under a Bad Sign - Wikipedia
notes: Albert King, Stax, August 1967; Jim Stewart credited; Wayne Jackson said Cropper and Al Jackson Jr. ran the sessions; Jackson on drums; Crosscut Saw is side one, track 2.

title: Soul Man (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Sam & Dave, Stax S-231, September 1967; recorded at Stax; on Soul Men; Al Jackson Jr. on drums.

title: Time Is Tight - Wikipedia
notes: For the film Up Tight (1968); single February 1969 (3:14, slower), the soundtrack's version 4:55 and faster; written by Jones, Jackson, Dunn and Cropper; Jackson on drums; No. 6 Hot 100, No. 4 UK.

title: Melting Pot (Booker T album) - Wikipedia
notes: Stax STS-2035, January 1971; recorded 1970 at Stax and the Record Plant, New York; produced by the band; Al Jackson Jr. on drums; the title track and Chicken Pox sampled in hip-hop.

title: Let's Stay Together (Al Green album) - Wikipedia
notes: Hi SH-32070, 31 January 1972; produced by Willie Mitchell at Royal Recording Studio, Memphis; drums: Howard Grimes and Al Jackson Jr., not split by track.

title: Let's Stay Together (Al Green song) - Wikipedia
notes: 1971; written by Al Green, Willie Mitchell and Al Jackson Jr.; No. 1 Hot 100, nine weeks No. 1 R&B. No personnel given.

title: Shake! Otis at Monterey - Wikipedia
notes: D.A. Pennebaker's 19-minute film (1987) of Otis Redding at Monterey Pop, 1967, backed by Booker T. & the M.G.'s: Shake, Respect, I've Been Loving You Too Long, Satisfaction, Try a Little Tenderness; cut short by rain and curfew.

title: Otis Redding at Monterey Pop, 17 June 1967 (Pennebaker footage, YouTube AqYWfxmAStU and NuJTUpJzLOw)
notes: Watched as contact sheets. The film's title card: 'Monterey California June 17 1967'. Jackson in a pale lime-yellow single-breasted jacket over a jade-green high-necked top, close-cropped hair, a thin moustache, at a white-wrapped kit with chrome hardware, a script 'R' on the bass drum's front head; Cropper and Dunn in olive-green suits. Close-ups of him at the kit at 3:28-3:33 and 4:14-4:21 of NuJTUpJzLOw.

title: Southern soul - Wikipedia
notes: 'Southern soul or country soul is a type of soul and country music that emerged from the Southern United States.' Late 1950s, peak in the 1960s; 12-bar and jump blues, country, early R&B and gospel; Stax with Booker T. & the MGs and Hi with Willie Mitchell in Memphis, FAME and the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section; Otis Redding, Sam & Dave, Wilson Pickett, Al Green, Aretha Franklin; its rhythmic drive a major influence on funk.
